Administering KoldFusion Server

Web Server and SSL

ColdFusion 4.5 left the web server to IIS or Netscape Enterprise Server. KoldFusion brings its own, and this page (a KoldFusion extra) sets how it handles connections and secure sockets.

Go there: Open the Web Server and SSL page (or inside the frameset)

HTTP connections

KoldFusion speaks HTTP/1.1. A browser can keep one connection open and send request after request over it (and HTTP/1.0 browsers that send Connection: Keep-Alive, as Netscape 4 and Internet Explorer 4 did, get the same treatment). Requests may be pipelined; the answers come back in order. Every answer carries an exact Content-Length, HEAD requests get the headers without the body, request bodies may be sent chunked, and Expect: 100-continue is honored. Static files carry Last-Modified and ETag, so a browser that already has a file gets a short "304 Not Modified"; changing the page zoom counts as a change to every HTML file.

Setting Default What it does
Allow persistent (keep-alive) connections on Off answers every request with Connection: close, like 1999.
Close idle connections after N seconds 15 How long an open connection may wait for its next request.
... and after N requests 100 Requests per connection before the server asks the browser to reconnect.
Request header timeout 20 seconds The whole request header (and the SSL handshake) must arrive in this time. A client that trickles one byte at a time ("slowloris") is cut off with "408 Request Timeout". Request bodies get 30 seconds plus a second for every 64 KB.
Maximum connections 400 Open connections at once; more are refused with "503 Service Unavailable". Above three quarters of the limit, responses close their connection instead of keeping it alive.

The keep-alive settings apply to new connections straight away. The request limit on Server Settings still counts templates being run, not open connections, so idle keep-alive connections never block the queue.

Secure Sockets Layer

When the OpenSSL libraries (libssl.so.3, or 1.1) are installed, KoldFusion also listens for https:// requests, on port 8543 unless you choose another. No SSL library is needed to build KoldFusion; it looks for one when it starts, and if there is none the page says so and the secure listener stays off.

Setting Default What it does
Enable the secure listener on port on, 8543 kfserver --ssl-port PORT overrides the port for one run, and --ssl-port 0 turns the listener off.
Server certificate / Private key kfroot/ssl/kfserver.crt, .key PEM files. A certificate chain file may hold intermediate certificates after the server's own.
Ask browsers for a client certificate off Any client certificate is accepted and shows up in CGI.CERT_SUBJECT, CGI.CERT_ISSUER, CGI.CERT_SERIALNUMBER and CGI.CERT_FLAGS.
Verify server certificates in CFHTTP on CFHTTP checks an https:// server's certificate against the system's certificate authorities, and trusts this server's own certificate. Turn it off to accept anything, or use CHECKCERTIFICATE="No" on one tag.

Changes to the listener take effect when the server restarts; use Restart Server... at the bottom of the page.

The certificate

On its first start KoldFusion asks /usr/bin/openssl for a self-signed certificate: subject CN=localhost, O=Gibson Mainframe Co., valid for ten years, for the names localhost, *.localhost, 127.0.0.1 and every virtual site (yowza.localhost and friends, each named outright because OpenSSL does not accept a wildcard directly below localhost). Generate Self-Signed Certificate makes a fresh one, and the secure listener switches to it at once. To make one by hand:

openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -sha256 -days 3650 -nodes \
  -keyout kfroot/ssl/kfserver.key -out kfroot/ssl/kfserver.crt \
  -subj "/CN=localhost/O=Gibson Mainframe Co." \
  -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:localhost,DNS:*.localhost,IP:127.0.0.1"

Browsers warn about a self-signed certificate. Either click through, as everyone did in 1999, or import kfserver.crt as a trusted authority; curl --cacert kfroot/ssl/kfserver.crt https://localhost:8543/ works without warnings. A virtual site can have its own certificate: put <name>.localhost.crt and <name>.localhost.key in kfroot/ssl/, and browsers that send the host name (SNI, which every browser since about 2006 does) get it.

What pages see

Variable Plain HTTP Over SSL
CGI.HTTPS off on
CGI.SERVER_PORT_SECURE 0 1
CGI.SERVER_PORT 8500 8543
CGI.CERT_KEYSIZE, CGI.HTTPS_KEYSIZE (empty) Bits of the session key, for example 256
CGI.CERT_SECRETKEYSIZE, CGI.HTTPS_SECRETKEYSIZE (empty) Bits of the server's private key, for example 2048
CGI.CERT_SERVER_SUBJECT, CGI.CERT_SERVER_ISSUER (empty) The server certificate's subject and issuer, such as CN=localhost, O=Gibson Mainframe Co.
CGI.CERT_SUBJECT, CGI.CERT_ISSUER, CGI.CERT_SERIALNUMBER, CGI.CERT_COOKIE (empty) The client certificate, when one was asked for and sent
CGI.CERT_FLAGS (empty) 0 without a client certificate, 1 with one, 3 when its issuer is not trusted

These are the names IIS 4.0 used. The redirects between virtual sites keep the scheme and port: a link from https://yowza.localhost:8543/ to another site stays on https and port 8543.
